title: Chapter 1 — Philosophical Method Among the Americans
paragraphs: I think that in no country in the civilized world is less attention paid to philosophy than in the United States. The Americans have no philosophical school of their own, and they care little for all the schools into which Europe is divided, whose very names are scarcely known to them. Nevertheless, it is easy to see that almost all the inhabitants of the United States conduct their understanding in the same manner, and govern it by the same rules; that is, without ever having taken the trouble to define the rules of a philosophical method, they possess one, common to the whole people. To escape the bondage of system and habit, of family maxims, class opinions, and, to some extent, national prejudices; to accept tradition only as a source of information, and existing facts only as a lesson useful for doing otherwise, and doing better; to seek the reason of things for oneself, and in oneself alone; to aim at results without being bound to means, and to reach the substance through the form — such are the principal features of what I will call the philosophical method of the Americans. But if I go further, and look among these features for the one that dominates and includes almost all the rest, I find that in most operations of the mind, each American appeals to the individual exercise of his own understanding alone. America is therefore one of the countries in the world where philosophy is least studied, and where the precepts of Descartes are best applied. Nor is this surprising. The Americans do not read the works of Descartes, because their social condition deters them from speculative studies; but they follow his maxims because that very social condition naturally disposes their understanding to adopt them. Amid the continual movement that stirs a democratic community, the tie that unites one generation to another is loosened or broken; every man readily loses the trace of the ideas of his forefathers, or takes no care about them. Nor can men living in this state of society derive their belief from the opinions of the class to which they belong, for, so to speak, there are no longer any classes, or those that still exist are composed of such mobile elements that the body can never exercise real control over its members. As for the influence the intelligence of one man has on that of another, it must necessarily be very limited in a country where the citizens, placed on a footing of general similarity, are all closely in view of one another, and where, since no signs of incontestable greatness or superiority are perceived in any one of them, they are constantly brought back to their own reason as the most obvious and nearest source of truth. It is not only confidence in this or that man that is then destroyed, but the taste for trusting the ipse dixit of any man whatsoever. Everyone shuts himself up in his own breast, and from that point presumes to judge the world.

The practice the Americans have of fixing the standard of their judgment in themselves alone leads them into other habits of mind. As they see that they succeed in resolving, without help, all the little difficulties their practical life presents, they readily conclude that everything in the world can be explained, and that nothing in it transcends the limits of the understanding. So they fall to denying what they cannot comprehend, which leaves them little faith in whatever is extraordinary, and an almost insurmountable distaste for whatever is supernatural. Since it is on their own testimony that they are accustomed to rely, they like to perceive the object that engages their attention with extreme clearness. They therefore strip off as much as possible of whatever covers it, rid themselves of whatever separates them from it, and remove whatever conceals it from sight, in order to view it more closely and in the broad light of day. This cast of mind soon leads them to despise forms, which they regard as useless and inconvenient veils placed between them and the truth.

The Americans, then, have not needed to extract their philosophical method from books; they have found it in themselves. The same thing may be observed in what has happened in Europe. This same method has only been established and made popular in Europe as the condition of society has become more equal, and men have grown more like each other. Let us consider for a moment the sequence of the periods in which this change may be traced. In the sixteenth century the Reformers subjected some of the dogmas of the ancient faith to the scrutiny of private judgment, but still withheld from it the judgment of all the rest. In the seventeenth century, Bacon in the natural sciences, and Descartes in philosophy in the strict sense of the term, abolished recognized formulas, destroyed the empire of tradition, and overthrew the authority of the schools. The philosophers of the eighteenth century, generalizing at last the same principle, undertook to submit to the private judgment of each man all the objects of his belief.

Who does not see that Luther, Descartes, and Voltaire employed the same method, and that they differed only in the greater or lesser extent to which they professed it should be used? Why did the Reformers confine themselves so closely within the circle of religious ideas? Why did Descartes, choosing to apply his method only to certain matters, though he had made it fit to be applied to all, declare that men could judge for themselves in matters philosophical but not in matters political? How did it happen that in the eighteenth century those general applications were all at once drawn from this same method, which Descartes and his predecessors had either not perceived or had rejected? And to what, lastly, is it to be attributed that at this period the method we are speaking of suddenly emerged from the schools, to penetrate into society and become the common standard of intelligence; and that, after it had become popular among the French, it was openly adopted or secretly followed by all the nations of Europe?

The philosophical method here designated may have been engendered in the sixteenth century; it may have been more accurately defined and more extensively applied in the seventeenth; but neither in the one nor in the other could it be commonly adopted. Political laws, the condition of society, and the habits of mind that derive from these causes were still opposed to it. It was discovered at a time when men were beginning to equalize and assimilate their conditions. It could be generally followed only in ages when those conditions had at last become nearly equal, and men nearly alike.

The philosophical method of the eighteenth century is therefore not only French, but democratic; and this explains why it was so readily adopted throughout Europe, where it has contributed so powerfully to change the face of society. It is not because the French changed their former opinions and altered their former manners that they convulsed the world; it is because they were the first to generalize and bring to light a philosophical method with whose help it became easy to attack all that was old, and to open a path to all that was new.

If it is asked why, at the present day, this same method is more rigorously followed and more frequently applied by the French than by the Americans, although the principle of equality is no less complete, and of more ancient date, among the latter people, the fact may be attributed to two circumstances that must first be clearly understood. It must never be forgotten that religion gave birth to Anglo-American society. In the United States religion is therefore intertwined with all the habits of the nation and all the feelings of patriotism, from which it derives a peculiar force. To this powerful reason another of no less intensity may be added: in America religion has, as it were, laid down its own limits. Religious institutions have remained wholly distinct from political institutions, so that the former laws have been easily changed while the former belief has remained unshaken. Christianity has therefore kept a strong hold on the public mind in America; and, I would particularly remark, its sway is not only that of a philosophical doctrine adopted on inquiry, but of a religion which is believed without discussion. In the United States, Christian sects are infinitely diversified and perpetually modified; but Christianity itself is a fact so irresistibly established that no one undertakes either to attack or to defend it. The Americans, having accepted the principal doctrines of the Christian religion without inquiry, are obliged to accept in the same way a great number of moral truths originating in it and connected with it. Hence the activity of individual analysis is restrained within narrow limits, and many of the most important of human opinions are removed from the range of its influence.

The second circumstance I have alluded to is this: the social condition and constitution of the Americans are democratic, but they have not had a democratic revolution. They arrived on the soil they occupy in nearly the condition in which we see them today; and this is of very considerable importance.

There are no revolutions that do not shake existing belief, weaken authority, and throw doubt over commonly received ideas. The effect of all revolutions is therefore, more or less, to surrender men to their own guidance, and to open to every man's mind a void and almost unlimited range of speculation. When equality of conditions succeeds a prolonged conflict between the different classes that composed the older society, envy, hatred, and uncharitableness, pride, and exaggerated self-confidence are apt to seize the human heart and plant their sway there for a time. This, independently of equality itself, tends powerfully to divide men — to make them mistrust the judgment of others, and to seek the light of truth nowhere but in their own understandings. Everyone then tries to be his own sufficient guide, and makes it his boast to form his own opinions on all subjects. Men are no longer bound together by ideas, but by interests; and it is as if human opinions were reduced to a kind of intellectual dust, scattered on every side, unable to collect, unable to cohere.

So that independence of mind which equality implies is never so great, nor ever appears so excessive, as at the moment when equality is beginning to establish itself, and in the course of that painful labor by which it is established. That kind of intellectual freedom which equality may give must therefore be very carefully distinguished from the anarchy that revolution brings. Each of these two things must be considered separately, so as not to conceive exaggerated hopes or fears of the future.

I believe that the men who will live under the new forms of society will make frequent use of their private judgment; but I am far from thinking that they will often abuse it. This is attributable to a cause more generally applicable to all democratic countries, and one which, in the long run, must necessarily restrain in them the independence of individual speculation within fixed, and sometimes narrow, limits. I will proceed to point out this cause in the next chapter.
